title: Chaffee County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Chaffee County the median well depth is 105 ft with a 12 gpm median yield. See how that affects drilling cost and water reliability for your property.
h1: Water wells in Chaffee County, Colorado
intro_html: Chaffee County wells are mostly in fractured mountain bedrock, so depth and yield can change a lot from Salida to Buena Vista to Nathrop. Still, with over 7,400 wells reporting depths and more than 4,300 with test yields, there is enough data to set realistic expectations on how deep you are likely to drill and how much water you can count on.

sections.heading: How deep wells usually run in Chaffee County
sections.html: Across Chaffee County, the median well depth is 105 feet, with the middle half of wells between 60 and 196 feet. That means a lot of homes hit water in the first couple hundred feet, but you do see some deeper holes. About 43% of wells are under 100 feet, another 44% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 11% between 300 and 600 feet, and only 1% go deeper than 600 feet. The deepest well on record is 1,000 feet. In this fractured-bedrock setting, a driller will usually bid with a depth allowance into that 100–200 foot range, but be clear on the per-foot price in case you end up on the deeper side.

sections.heading: Well yield: how much water you actually get
sections.html: Yield in Chaffee County is generally solid for single-family homes. The median reported pump yield is 12.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells come in between 9.0 and 15.0 gpm. About 69% of wells produce between 5 and 15 gpm and another 25% are above 15 gpm. Only 6% fall between 1 and 5 gpm, and there are no reported wells under 1 gpm in the dataset. For a typical exempt household-use well with the standard 35 gpm pumping limit, these production rates are more than enough, but if you’re planning irrigation or livestock you still want to review individual well permits nearby.

sections.heading: Water levels and long-term trend in the county
sections.html: Static water levels in Chaffee County are moderate. The median depth to water is 55 feet below ground, with the middle half between 32 and 110 feet. Looking at the measurements over time, median water levels were about 33–34 feet in the 1970s and 1980s, then shifted to 42 feet in the 1990s and 48 feet in the 2000s. In the 2010s the median reached 60 feet, then eased to 56 feet in the 2020s. That points to a gradual long-term decline compared to the 1970s, typical of growing domestic use in mountain valleys, but not a sudden crash. Still, plan on a pump set well below the static level for reliability.

sections.heading: Who has been drilling here and when
sections.html: Chaffee County has a long well history, with 10,201 permits in the state’s records and 6,594 recorded as constructed. Drilling picked up heavily in the 1970s when 1,043 permits were issued, then stayed strong: 989 in the 1980s, 2,043 in the 1990s, and 2,139 in the 2000s. The 2010s saw 1,270 permits, and there are already 937 in the 2020s, with the newest permit showing in 2026. Most wells are for domestic or household use at 85%, with stock use at 6%, monitoring at 6%, and irrigation at 1%. American Drilling Service, Mccoy Drilling Inc, and Whitewater Systems show up most often on the county’s permits.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Chaffee County
sections.html: Here the ground is mainly fractured granite and gneiss, drilled at a typical rate of about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s 105-foot median depth, that puts the borehole itself around $6,800–$10,500. Once you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished residential well usually ends up in the $12,800–$22,500 range at that depth. Because the middle half of wells runs from 60 to 196 feet, it is smart to budget toward the higher end of that range and make sure your driller contract spells out what happens on cost if they need to go significantly deeper.

sections.heading: Geology, contamination risks, and low-yield pockets
sections.html: Almost all wells here are completed in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 9,887 wells in that category, and only a small share in Alluvial or Quaternary Alluvium. Fractured rock is unpredictable: two wells a few hundred feet apart can have different depths and yields, and a small minority will still be marginal despite decent countywide averages. Around Chaffee County there are mapped risks you should be aware of: 16 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 1,310 historic mine features, and 12 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Before you buy, review state maps and well logs around your lot, and plan adequate separation between your well, septic system, and any historic mining disturbances.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a well lot in Chaffee County
sections.html: With 7,436 wells reporting depths and 4,375 reporting yields, there is plenty of local data to lean on when you look at land from Salida to Buena Vista, Johnson Village, Nathrop, Maysville, or Garfield. For an existing home, pull the well permit and test yield, and consider a water-quality test if you are near mapped PFAS or historic mine sites. On vacant land, look at neighboring well depths and yields and assume you might end up closer to the deep side of the 60–196 foot middle range. Factor well and septic costs into your build budget, and talk early with your driller and engineer about any augmentation or water-rights issues in over-appropriated basins.
